# Results — Study 917 (Stale NAV) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim: a US-listed
single-country ETF tracks a market that is **shut** while Wall Street trades, so its price
is stale with respect to the US session that just happened and should **catch up** the next
day. The test: regress the fund's day-`t+1` total return on **SPY**'s day-`t` total return
(HAC / Newey-West), per fund and per era; then trade it — long the fund for the day-`t+1`
return whenever SPY's day-`t` return sat in the **top decile** of its own expanding history.
One execution lag (signal formed through the close of `t`, position on for the `t+1`
return). Daily total-return closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`), 10 bps one-way cost,
every leg measured **excess-of-cash**. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current month is
dropped). Every "net of SPY" figure is reported under **two** hedges — a unit hedge (nothing
fitted; the headline) and a fitted contemporaneous beta (in-sample, a labelled diagnostic) —
because the unit-beta shortcut turns out to be load-bearing (§1a).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY + EWJ, EWG, FXI, EWA, EWU | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-30 | 8,411 | Fingerprint `42e35a0143ca` |

The country funds start 1996-03-18 (FXI 2004-10-08), so the regression samples are 7,619
observations for EWJ/EWG/EWA/EWU and 5,464 for FXI. **Cash = `^IRX`** (13-week T-bill
discount rate), compounded daily and lagged one day — a **PROXY**, since `^IRX` is an index
and not an investable fund; BIL (the tradable cash ETF) re-runs the headline below over its
shorter 2007+ window. **Total return throughout** (`auto_adjust=True`): country ETFs pay
large, lumpy distributions and a price-only tape would put a sawtooth straight into the
daily returns being regressed. Survivorship: all six tickers are **survivors** trading
today; no delisted country fund is in the panel, which if anything flatters the tape.

## 1. The predictive regression — the sign is wrong

`r_fund[t+1] = a + b · r_SPY[t]`, HAC standard errors. The catch-up story predicts **b > 0**.

| Fund | n | raw *b* | HAC *t* | *b* net of SPY (unit hedge) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| EWJ (Japan) | 7,619 | **−0.111** | **−5.85** | −0.027 | −1.51 |
| EWG (Germany) | 7,619 | −0.060 | −2.25 | +0.024 | +1.58 |
| FXI (China/HK) | 5,464 | **−0.263** | **−6.54** | **−0.160** | **−4.30** |
| EWA (Australia) | 7,619 | −0.073 | −1.75 | +0.011 | +0.45 |
| EWU (UK) | 7,619 | −0.056 | −2.13 | +0.028 | +2.01 |
| *domestic control* — SPY on **itself** | 8,409 | **−0.082** | **−3.51** | — | — |

Every raw slope is **negative**: a strong US day is followed by a country fund that gives
part of it *back*, not one that catches up. Part of that is not about timezones at all —
**SPY itself** reverses at the same horizon (*b* = −0.082, *t* = −3.51), and a country ETF
inherits that reversal through its US beta. The right-hand column nets it out with
`(r_fund[t+1] − r_SPY[t+1]) = a + b · r_SPY[t]`.

### 1a. The unit-beta ASSUMPTION, and what happens when you drop it

Subtracting **one** unit of SPY assumes each fund's contemporaneous US beta is exactly 1.
It is not — it runs **0.75 (EWJ) to 1.16 (FXI)** — so the unit hedge leaves `(β − 1)` units
of SPY in the residual and re-imports `(β − 1) × (−0.082)` of the market's own reversal.
That shortcut is **load-bearing**, so the table below drops it: β is refit on the same
sample (`r_fund[t] = a + β·r_SPY[t]`) and the fund is hedged at that ratio. The
decomposition `b_raw = β × b_domestic + b_hedged` is an exact identity, tested in
`tests/test_strategy.py`.

| Fund | β (contemp.) | raw *b* | = confound `β × −0.082` | share of raw | + hedged *b* | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| EWJ | 0.754 | −0.111 | −0.062 | 56% | **−0.048** | **−3.19** |
| EWG | 0.993 | −0.060 | −0.082 | 137% | +0.023 | +1.54 |
| FXI | 1.161 | −0.263 | −0.096 | 36% | **−0.143** | **−3.65** |
| EWA | 0.921 | −0.073 | −0.076 | 104% | +0.004 | +0.17 |
| EWU | 0.866 | −0.056 | −0.071 | 128% | +0.017 | +1.20 |

> **CAVEAT:** this β is **fitted in-sample and applied in-sample**. It is a diagnostic, not
> a tradable rule, and it never stamps a badge — which is why the headline column stays the
> unfitted unit hedge. It is reported because honesty requires showing that the shortcut
> moves numbers.

Two things change, and neither helps the claim:

1. **The confound does not "explain most of it" uniformly.** It *over*-explains EWG, EWA
   and EWU (104–137%: those three reverse *less* than their beta says they should), covers
   just **56%** of EWJ and only **36%** of FXI.
2. **Under the fitted hedge, two funds — not one — clear the |*t*| ≥ 2.58 Bonferroni bar:
   EWJ (−3.19) and FXI (−3.65). Both are NEGATIVE.** Correctly hedging makes the *reversal*
   sharper, never the catch-up: **no fund has a positive timezone slope under either hedge**,
   and the largest positive anywhere is EWG's +1.54, well inside noise. The claim fails the
   same way in both specifications, which is the only reason a single badge covers both.

## 2. Era cut (split 2010-01-01) — the one exception dies

Net-of-SPY slope, so this is the timezone-specific component only. Both hedges are shown;
in the fitted column β is **refit within each era** (never borrowed across the split).

| Fund | early, unit hedge *b* (*t*) | early, fitted hedge *b* (*t*) | late, unit hedge *b* (*t*) | late, fitted hedge *b* (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| EWJ | −0.059 (−2.98) | **−0.076 (−3.85)** | +0.015 (+0.56) | −0.010 (−0.55) |
| EWG | +0.036 (+1.69) | +0.033 (+1.52) | +0.008 (+0.37) | +0.013 (+0.57) |
| FXI | **−0.347 (−7.31)** | **−0.288 (−5.63)** | −0.046 (−1.54) | −0.055 (−1.90) |
| EWA | +0.063 (+2.02) | +0.048 (+1.50) | −0.057 (−1.68) | −0.047 (−1.53) |
| EWU | +0.040 (+1.99) | +0.029 (+1.40) | +0.012 (+0.64) | +0.002 (+0.12) |

This is the decisive cut, and it says the same thing under either hedge. The two slopes
that clear Bonferroni on the full sample are **entirely pre-2010**: FXI's is its illiquid
2004–2009 childhood (*t* = −5.63 fitted, on 1,317 days) and is **gone** after 2010
(*t* = −1.90); EWJ's early *t* = −3.85 collapses to **−0.55**. In the modern era **not one
fund clears |*t*| = 2 in either hedge, in either direction.** This is what fair-value
pricing and round-the-clock ETF arbitrage killing an effect looks like — except that the
effect they killed was *over-reaction and reversal* (Levy & Lieberman 2013), never the
catch-up the folklore promises.

## 3. The tradable rule — equal-weight basket of the five funds

Long the basket for the day-`t+1` return after a top-decile SPY day; cash otherwise;
10 bps one-way on every position change. 819 trigger days (10.7% of the tape), 1,402
position changes.

| Arm | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Long rule (the claim)** | **−0.701** | −6.15% | 8.5% | −3.77 |
| Short mirror | −0.419 | −3.85% | 8.5% | −2.32 |
| Buy & hold the basket *(untraded — pays no cost)* | **+0.298** | +4.19% | 21.5% | +1.89 |

- Trigger-day basket excess return: **−4.92 bps/day** (HAC *t* = −0.82); every other day
  **+3.45 bps/day**; difference −8.37 bps (Welch *t* = −1.41). This figure is **gross of
  trading cost** — the claim's best case; the cost only enters the Sharpe rows.
- **Net of SPY's same-day move — the timezone-specific part: −1.30 bps/day (HAC *t* = −0.39)**
  under the unit hedge, **−1.55 bps/day (*t* = −0.46)** at the fitted β of 0.906. Nothing,
  either way: the hedge ratio that mattered for a single fund's slope is immaterial here.
- Block bootstrap (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks): trigger-day mean 95% CI
  **[−19.75, +6.63] bps** — straddles zero, 77.3% of resamples negative.

Two disclosures on this table. **Costs are one-sided**: the rule pays 10 bps on each of its
1,402 position changes, buy-and-hold pays nothing. Charging B&H a round trip would cost it
~2 bps *in total* over 30 years, and the asymmetry runs **against** the claim, so it is left
in rather than tuned away. And the HAC *t* on trigger-day means is computed on a
**non-contiguous subsample** — the Bartlett lags pair observations adjacent in the
subsample, not in the calendar; it is an approximation, and the era cut plus the block
bootstrap (which do respect calendar time) are what the verdict actually leans on.

## 4. Robustness

**Era cut on the rule** (each era re-derives its own expanding decile):

| Era | n | trigger-day mean | HAC *t* | net-of-SPY *b* (*t*) | long exSharpe | B&H exSharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1996–2009 | 3,472 | +3.95 bps | +0.53 | −0.008 (−0.40) | −0.447 | +0.279 |
| 2010–2026 | 4,146 | −13.17 bps | −1.58 | −0.014 (−0.83) | −0.927 | +0.323 |

The trigger-day mean flips sign between eras and clears |*t*| = 2 in neither.

**Cost sweep** (one-way, bps of NAV, both directions):

| Cost | Long exSharpe (*t*) | Short mirror (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 (gross) | −0.157 (−0.86) | **+0.127 (+0.70)** |
| 5 | −0.430 (−2.34) | −0.146 (−0.81) |
| **10 (baseline)** | −0.701 (−3.77) | −0.419 (−2.32) |
| 25 | −1.494 (−7.73) | −1.224 (−6.80) |
| 50 | −2.699 (−12.95) | −2.465 (−13.29) |

The mirror trade is the only arm that is ever positive, and only **gross** (+0.127,
*t* = +0.70 — nowhere near |*t*| = 2). It is under water by 5 bps one-way, before any borrow.

**Borrow sweep** for the short mirror (annual fee on the short leg, an ASSUMPTION; the
long rule has no short leg and pays none): −0.419 at 0%, −0.425 at 0.5%, −0.444 at 2%,
−0.482 at 5%. Borrow is not what kills it; the spread already did.

**Threshold sweep** (what counts as a strong US day): top 20% −3.13 bps (*t* = −0.87),
top 10% −4.92 (−0.82), top 5% −7.02 (−0.72), top 1% −60.57 (*t* = −2.18, only 109 days).
The one significant cell is the 1% tail — extreme US up-days, which are crisis days when
*everything* mean-reverts — and it is again the *opposite* of the claim.

**Conservative variant** (refuse to assume an at-the-close execution on the signal day and
wait one extra day): trigger-day mean **+0.70 bps (*t* = +0.13)**. Nothing survives a day.

**BIL cross-check** (tradable cash leg, 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30): trigger-day mean
−28.56 bps (*t* = −2.59), long exSharpe −1.037 vs buy-and-hold +0.244 — the same picture,
sharper, because BIL's window is dominated by the 2008–09 reversal regime.

**Synthetic control** (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp): on a panel with a
*planted* +0.250 catch-up beta the regression recovers **+0.249** (mean HAC *t* = +18.0) and
the trigger-day mean is +53.6 bps (*t* = +11.5); on eight null seeds with the identical
contemporaneous correlation the recovered beta is **−0.004** (sd 0.007) and the max |*t*|
across five funds clears 2 on 1 seed in 8 — the expected false-positive rate. The harness
finds a real catch-up when one exists and stays quiet when it does not.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** The stale-price catch-up is not on the tape, in any fund, in any era,
  under either hedge. Every raw slope is **negative**, and part of that is SPY's own
  next-day reversal (*b* = −0.082, *t* = −3.51) arriving through the fund's US beta. Net of
  it, **no fund shows a positive timezone loading anywhere**: the largest positive slope in
  the study is EWG's +1.54 under the fitted hedge, well inside noise, against a five-fund
  Bonferroni bar of |*t*| ≥ 2.58. What *does* clear that bar clears it with the **wrong
  sign** — FXI (*t* = −4.30 unit, −3.65 fitted) and, once the unit-beta shortcut is dropped,
  EWJ (−3.19) — and **both die at the era cut** (FXI −1.90, EWJ −0.55 after 2010), so even
  the anti-claim is a pre-2010 artifact, not a live effect. On the basket the
  timezone-specific trigger-day return is **−1.30 bps/day (*t* = −0.39)** at unit hedge and
  **−1.55 (*t* = −0.46)** at the fitted β, with a bootstrap CI straddling zero; it flips
  sign across eras, and it is **+0.70 bps (*t* = +0.13)** if you wait one more day to trade.
  A "Real" stamp would need a robust |*t*| ≥ 2 **in the claimed direction** on this tape;
  the claimed direction never reaches |*t*| = 1.6 in any specification run here.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** The rule as stated loses money outright (excess Sharpe −0.70
  net, versus **+0.30** for simply holding the same basket): you spend 10.7% of the tape
  paying two spreads a round trip for a day that is, if anything, slightly worse than
  average. The mirror short — the only arm the data leans toward — is +0.127 excess Sharpe
  **gross**, *t* = +0.70, and is under water by 5 bps one-way, before borrow, on five ETFs
  that are anything but free to short.
- **Scope limit, stated plainly.** This is a **close-to-close** test on US-listed ETFs,
  which trade continuously in New York and therefore price the US session *as it happens*;
  the stale-NAV literature's original victim was the once-a-day *mutual fund* NAV strike,
  which no longer exists in this form. Finding nothing here is the modern-market answer to
  the old question, not a refutation of the 1990s evidence.
